title: CSS Syntax and Rules
summary: A CSS rule names what to style and lists the changes inside curly brackets.
introduction: A CSS rule names what to style and lists the changes inside curly brackets. Read one rule like a short instruction: choose h1, then make its colour blue. Learn where the colon and semicolon go.
learningObjectives: Name the parts of a CSS rule: selector, declaration block, property and value
Write valid declarations with the correct separators and comments
Use shorthand properties and recognise when the browser has ignored a declaration

rows: Decides which elements the rule applies to
The aspect of the element you are changing

blocks.text: A colon separates the property from its value and a semicolon ends the declaration. The semicolon after the last declaration is technically optional, but always write it: the moment you add another declaration below, a missing semicolon breaks both lines, as you will see at the end of this lesson. Property names are case-insensitive (`COLOR` works) but the convention is lowercase everywhere.

A comma lets one rule target several selectors, which avoids repeating identical declarations. And several rules can match the same element: their declarations are merged, so the heading below gets its typeface and colour from the first rule and its size from the second.

blocks.text: When two rules set the *same* property on the same element, the cascade decides. The short version, enough for now: a more specific selector wins, and between equally specific selectors the one written later wins. [Specificity, Inheritance and the Cascade](/tutorials/css/specificity-cascade) covers the full rules.

Comments start with `/*` and end with `*/`; they can span several lines and may appear anywhere a space can. Whitespace itself is ignored, so `h1{color:red}` and the four-line version mean the same thing. The convention most teams follow is one declaration per line, two spaces of indentation and a blank line between rules, because it makes diffs readable.

blocks.title: Comments
// is not a comment
blocks.text: Many languages use `//` for comments; CSS does not. A line such as `// color: red;` becomes part of a broken declaration, and because the browser reads until the next semicolon it can swallow the *next* declaration as well. Use `/* … */` only.

A **shorthand** sets several related properties (its *longhands*) in one declaration. `margin: 8px 16px;` sets the top and bottom margins to 8px and the left and right margins to 16px; `border: 1px solid #cbd5e1;` sets the width, style and colour of all four borders at once. Shorthands keep stylesheets short, with one catch: any longhand you leave out is reset to its default value, even if an earlier rule had set it.

blocks.title: A shorthand resets what you omit

blocks.text: What happens when you make a mistake

CSS was designed so that old browsers could skip features they did not understand, which means every browser follows the same error-recovery rules. An unknown property or an invalid value drops *that declaration* and keeps the rest of the rule. A missing semicolon glues two declarations into one invalid declaration, so both are lost. And if any selector in a comma-separated list is invalid, the *whole rule* is dropped.

blocks.title: Four declarations, one survivor
Result
blocks.content: The paragraph is green. Its font size and line height stay at their defaults, and the browser reports no error.

blocks.text: This is why the developer tools matter so much for CSS. In the *Styles* (Chrome, Edge) or *Rules* (Firefox) panel, ignored declarations are shown struck through with a small warning icon, and hovering the icon tells you why. Make a habit of checking there before rewriting a rule.

Modern CSS lets you write a rule inside another rule; the inner selector is combined with the outer one. The example below is equivalent to three flat rules: `.card`, `.card h2` and `.card:hover`. All current browsers support nesting. The rest of this tutorial mostly writes flat rules so that every snippet can be pasted anywhere, but you will meet nesting in real projects.

questions.question: What happens to `p { font-weight: heavy; color: green; }` in the browser?
questions.explanation: `heavy` is not a valid `font-weight` value, so that declaration alone is dropped. The valid `color: green;` declaration is still applied.
options: Only the invalid `font-weight` declaration is ignored; the paragraph is green
The browser shows an error dialog

questions.question: `h1, h2 { color: navy; }` applies the colour to both h1 and h2 elements.
questions.explanation: A comma in a selector creates a selector list; the declarations apply to every element matched by any selector in the list.
